title: Why "the Way"?
question: When Jesus says no one comes to the Father except through Him, what does He mean by being the only way, truth, and life?
blurb: Jesus calls Himself the road to the Father, and the rest of Scripture shows us where that road leads.

branches.note: Just after, Jesus says whoever has seen Him has seen the Father, so He is the way because He shows us the Father directly.
Peter echoes the same exclusivity: salvation is found in no one else, for there is no other name by which we must be saved.
There is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who alone bridges the gap.

branches.text: Jesus does not say He shows the way or teaches truth; He says He IS the way, the truth, and the life, so reaching the Father is about a Person, not a path or program.
The three terms hold together: He is the way to the Father precisely because He is also the truth and the life, and no one comes to the Father except through Him.

title: Why "the LORD is my shepherd"?
question: If the LORD is my shepherd, what does He actually do for me that means I shall not want?
blurb: David calls God his shepherd and lacks nothing. Trace what a shepherd does to see what that promise holds.

branches.note: David spells out the shepherd's care: leading to rest, water, and restored soul - the reason he lacks nothing.
Jesus calls Himself the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep.
The LORD tends His flock like a shepherd, gathering the lambs in His arms and gently leading.

branches.text: "I shall not want" doesn't promise every wish, but that with the shepherd providing, the sheep lacks no needed thing.

title: Made in God's Image?
question: What does Scripture show is true of people because they bear the image of God?
blurb: One verse says we bear God's image - trace what Scripture reveals that means for every human life.

branches.note: The verse just before: God says 'Let Us make man in Our image' and gives them rule over the creatures - the image comes with a role.
Bloodshed is judged 'for in His own image God has made mankind' - the image gives every life sacred worth.
The account is repeated: God made them in His likeness, 'male and female,' and blessed them and called them 'man.'
God blesses the image-bearers and tells them to be fruitful, fill the earth, and rule over it.

branches.text: The anchor states it three ways for emphasis: created in His image, in the image of God, male and female. Both man and woman together carry the image, by God's own making - not their own.

title: What Rest Does Jesus Give?
question: What is the weariness Jesus invites us to bring Him, and what kind of rest does He promise in return?
blurb: Jesus calls the weary and burdened to come to Him - and what He offers in return is more than a pause from work.

branches.note: The very next verse: rest comes by taking His yoke and learning from Him, who is gentle and humble - 'and you will find rest for your souls.'
He describes the new burden: 'For My yoke is easy and My burden is light.' Coming to Him is an exchange of burdens, not the end of all labor.
Jesus issues a parallel open invitation: 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink.' The cure for the weary is to come to Him.

branches.text: Notice who is invited: 'all you who are weary and burdened' - no qualifier but exhaustion itself. The condition for coming is simply that you need rest.
Jesus says 'I will give you rest' - rest is a gift He hands over, not a wage we earn. The action He asks of us is only to 'come.'

title: By His Wounds, Healed?
question: How can the suffering and wounds of one person bring peace and healing to others?
blurb: A wounded Servant takes the punishment we earned, so that His hurt becomes our healing and peace.

branches.text: The verse runs on a swap: 'our transgressions,' 'our iniquities,' the peace and healing that come to us are set against 'He was pierced,' 'He was crushed,' and the punishment that 'was upon Him.' His suffering is taken in place of ours.

branches.note: Peter applies this to Christ, who 'bore our sins in His body on the tree,' and repeats the promise: 'By His stripes you are healed.'
The exchange spelled out: the One who knew no sin was made sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.
The peace promised in the verse arrives: justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.
The next verse explains how: we all strayed like sheep, each to his own way, and 'the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all.'

title: Good in All Things?
question: For whom, and toward what end, does God work all things together for good?
blurb: A promise with an address: trace who it's for and the purpose it's aiming at.

branches.text: The promise is addressed: it is for "those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose" - not a blanket guarantee that every outcome will feel good, but that God bends all things toward good for His people.

branches.note: The very next verse names the "good" God aims at: to be conformed to the image of His Son.
Joseph tells his brothers: what they intended for evil, God intended for good - the principle lived out.
If God is for us, who can be against us? - the confidence this promise rests on.

branches.text: "All things" includes the suffering Paul has just been describing (8:18) - he is not denying hardship but saying nothing falls outside God's good purpose for His own.

title: Who Is the Word?
question: Who is "the Word" who was with God and was God in the beginning?
blurb: One verse hides a Person in plain sight, present at creation, with God and yet God. Follow the trail Scripture leaves.

branches.note: The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us, the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.
Through Him all things were made; without Him nothing was made that has been made. The Word is the agent of creation.
The rider on the white horse is named explicitly: His name is The Word of God.

branches.text: John opens with 'In the beginning,' the same words that open Genesis 1. The Word is both 'with God' (distinct from Him) and 'was God' (sharing His nature); and since all things were made through Him, He is not among the made things.

title: Peace Over Anxiety
question: What does God give in place of our anxiety, and how do we receive it?
blurb: Instead of worry, Paul points us to prayer—and to a peace that guards the heart beyond all understanding.

branches.text: The verse names the exchange directly: not just "stop worrying," but turn anxiety into prayer, petition, and thanksgiving—and God answers with a peace that guards heart and mind.

branches.note: The heart of bringing requests to God: cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.
Jesus' own word against worry—do not worry about tomorrow, for today has enough trouble of its own.
Jesus gives the very peace Paul describes: "My peace I give to you"—not as the world gives, so do not let your hearts be troubled.

branches.text: This peace "surpasses all understanding"—it isn't reasoned out by figuring things out, but given by God to guard our hearts and minds "in Christ Jesus."

title: Who Is "I AM"?
question: When God names Himself "I AM," what is He revealing about who He is?
blurb: At a burning bush, God answers Moses with a name unlike any other - and it still echoes across all of Scripture.

branches.text: God does not say "I was" or "I will be," but "I AM WHO I AM" - a name of pure, present existence. He simply IS.

branches.note: In the next breath God ties this name to His covenant: He is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob - "this is My name forever."
Jesus says, "Before Abraham was born, I am" - taking the very name God revealed at the bush onto His own lips.
"I am the Alpha and the Omega... who is and was and is to come" - the eternal, ever-present One the name "I AM" points to.

title: Whose Understanding?
question: What does it look like to trust the LORD with all my heart instead of leaning on my own understanding?
blurb: A daily look at what it means to hand God the whole heart and let Him straighten the road ahead.

branches.text: The trust is total ('all your heart') and it is paired with a refusal: do not lean on your own understanding. Both halves describe one posture of dependence on God.

branches.note: The one who trusts in the LORD is like a tree planted by the waters, unworried in a year of drought - the fruit of the trust Proverbs calls for.
Commit your way to the LORD and trust Him, and He will do it - echoing 'in all your ways acknowledge Him.'
God's thoughts and ways are higher than ours, which is why we lean on His understanding and not our own.

branches.text: The promise is not an easy road but a straight one: when we acknowledge Him in all our ways, He makes our paths straight.

title: Why Did Jesus Weep?
question: If Jesus knew He was about to raise Lazarus, what moved Him to weep at the tomb?
blurb: The shortest verse in the Bible holds the deepest comfort: God in the flesh, weeping with those who grieve.

branches.note: Just before weeping, Jesus saw Mary and the others weeping, and He was deeply moved in spirit and troubled.
Scripture calls us to weep with those who weep - exactly what Jesus does here.
Our high priest is able to sympathize with our weakness, sharing our sorrows.
Moments earlier He declared, 'I am the resurrection and the life' - His tears and His power stand side by side.

branches.text: His weeping was not despair or doubt. He already knew Lazarus would rise (John 11:11, 11:43-44); His tears reveal that real grief and certain hope can live together.

title: Plans to Give a Hope
question: What does God say His plans for His people are, and on what does He base that promise?
blurb: A famous promise spoken to exiles: the LORD knows His plans, and they are toward a future and a hope.

branches.text: These words were sent in a letter to people already carried away into exile in Babylon (Jeremiah 29:1, 4). God's promise of a future and a hope was spoken into hardship, not the absence of it.

branches.note: The very next verses: the people will call on Him and pray, and when they seek Him with all their heart, they will find Him. The promised plans come with an invitation to seek God.
The promise has a timeframe: when Babylon's seventy years are complete, God says He will attend to them and confirm His promise to restore them to this place.
The same heart of God beyond Israel's exile: He works all things together for the good of those who love Him and are called according to His purpose.

branches.text: The plans are God's ('the plans I have for you'). The hope rests on what He knows and intends, not on the people's circumstances or their ability to see the way out.

title: What Is Love Really Like?
question: What is the love that "never fails" actually like, as Scripture describes it?
blurb: Paul paints love not as a feeling but as patient, humble action - trace what it does and where it comes from.

branches.text: Paul describes love by what it does and refuses to do - patient, kind, not envious, boastful, proud, rude, self-seeking, or angry, keeping no record of wrongs. Love here is action, not mere feeling.

branches.note: The same passage's conclusion: 'Love never fails.' This is the enduring love the anchor verse is describing.
'God is love.' The source of the love described in the anchor - it reflects God's own character.
Jesus commands His followers to love one another as He has loved them - love that marks them as His.
Love demonstrated in action: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us - patient, self-giving love in the flesh.

title: The First Promise
question: In the curse on the serpent, what does God promise about the woman's seed and the enemy's defeat?
blurb: Spoken in Eden's darkest hour, the first hint of a coming Rescuer who will crush the serpent.

branches.note: God sends His Son, "born of a woman" - the promised seed arrives.
The Son of God appeared to destroy the works of the devil.
God will soon crush Satan under your feet - Eden's promise still echoing.

branches.text: The serpent strikes the heel (a wound), but the woman's seed crushes the head (a death blow) - a costly victory, not a stalemate.

branches.note: By sharing in flesh and blood, He through death destroyed the one holding the power of death.

title: Seek First His Kingdom
question: What does Jesus mean by seeking the kingdom of God first, and what does He promise will follow?
blurb: One command reorders everything we chase: put God's kingdom first, and watch what He promises to add.

branches.note: The verses just before name the very things we worry over - food, drink, clothing - and remind us the Father already knows we need them.
Earlier in the same teaching: where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. Seeking first reveals what we truly treasure.
No one can serve two masters. You cannot serve both God and money - so something must come first.

branches.text: Jesus does not say money and needs do not matter; He says the order matters. Put the kingdom and His righteousness first, and the 'all these things' fall into place under the Father's care.

title: Can a Heart Be Clean Again?
question: When sin has stained the heart, what is David asking God to do that only God can do?
blurb: David doesn't ask to fix himself; he asks God to create something new in him. What is that prayer really after?

branches.text: David asks God to 'create' a clean heart - a verb of divine making, not self-repair. He knows a clean heart is God's work to do in him, something he cannot manufacture himself.

branches.note: The prayer's opening: David pleads for mercy and to be washed and cleansed from his sin - the cleansing he longs for in verse 10.
God promises to give a new heart and a new spirit, removing the heart of stone - the same renewal David prays for.
If we confess our sins, God is faithful to forgive and cleanse us - the answer to David's plea for a clean heart.

branches.text: David pairs 'a clean heart' with 'a right spirit.' He longs not only to be cleansed of the past but renewed within - steadied and made faithful going forward.

title: What Faith Really Is
question: If faith is being sure of what we cannot see, what does the rest of Scripture show that confidence resting on?
blurb: Hebrews calls faith assurance and certainty - let's trace how the Bible itself fills out what that means.

branches.note: Faith is not blind: it believes God exists and rewards those who earnestly seek Him - and without it, it is impossible to please Him.
"We walk by faith, not by sight" - directly echoing Hebrews 11:1's 'certainty of what we do not see.'
Hope that is seen is no hope at all; we wait patiently for what we do not yet see - unfolding the 'hope' half of the anchor.
By faith we understand the universe was formed at God's command - so that what is seen came from what is unseen.

branches.text: The verse names two anchors of faith: 'what we hope for' (the future God promises) and 'what we do not see' (the unseen God Himself). Faith holds both as sure now.

title: What Does God Require?
question: If God has shown us what is good, what are the three things He asks of us in return?
blurb: God strips it all down to three simple, weighty words: do justice, love mercy, walk humbly with Him.

branches.note: God desires mercy and the knowledge of Him over mere sacrifice, just as Micah lifts the heart's posture above ritual offerings.
Jesus names justice, mercy, and faithfulness as the 'weightier matters' of the law, echoing Micah's three requirements.
'Administer true justice. Show loving devotion and compassion to one another' - the same call to just and merciful living.

branches.text: The verse pairs action with attitude: 'act justly' is what we do, 'love mercy' is what we delight in, and 'walk humbly' is how we relate to God Himself.
Micah 6 begins with God asking what offerings He wants (v.6-7); verse 8 answers that He wants a changed life, not more sacrifices.

title: How Did God Love Us?
question: What does God's love look like in action, and what does He give to those who believe?
blurb: One verse holds the heart of the gospel - trace how God's love gives, saves, and lasts forever.

branches.note: Love proven: Christ died for us while we were still sinners - showing the love John 3:16 describes is unearned.
Echoes the same act - God sent His one and only Son so that we might live through Him.
The very next verse: God sent the Son not to condemn the world, but to save it - love's purpose stated plainly.

branches.text: The verse pairs a gift ('He gave His one and only Son') with an invitation ('everyone who believes'). The love is God's; the response is ours.
Two destinies sit side by side: 'shall not perish' versus 'have eternal life.' Belief in the Son is what moves a person from one to the other.

title: But If Not
question: What kind of faith trusts God even when He might not rescue?
blurb: Three men face the furnace with a faith that bows to no idol, whether God delivers them or not.

branches.text: Their faith has two parts: God is able to deliver, AND even if He does not, they still will not worship the idol. Obedience is not conditional on rescue.

branches.note: God meets them inside the fire: a fourth figure walks with them in the flames, unbound and unharmed.
Why they refuse to bow: 'You shall have no other gods before Me.' Their stand flows straight from the first commandment.
Job voices the same 'but if not' trust: 'Though He slay me, I will hope in Him.'

branches.text: Their answer to the king (v.16) is that they need no defense. They have already settled the question of whom they serve before the outcome is known.

title: Why Be Still?
question: What truth about God lets us stop striving and rest, even when nations rage and the earth shakes?
blurb: A command to be still in the middle of chaos - and the reason it's possible: God Himself.

branches.note: The Psalm opens here: God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble - the ground for being still.
The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still. Stillness rests on God acting, not us striving.
By repentance and rest you would be saved; your strength would lie in quiet confidence - the same posture of rest before God.

branches.text: Being still is not passivity but trust: it is paired with 'know that I am God.' The stillness flows from recognizing who He is.
The verse twice declares 'I will be exalted' - over the nations and over the earth. We can rest because the outcome is His to secure, not ours.

title: How Does God Prove His Love?
question: When did God show His love for us, and what did it cost Him?
blurb: God didn't wait for us to clean up first. See the timing and the cost that proved His love.

branches.text: The proof is in the timing: 'while we were still sinners.' God's love came first, before we had earned anything or turned back to Him.

branches.note: Love measured by the gift: God gave His one and only Son for the world.
Love is not that we loved God, but that He loved us first and sent His Son.
Jesus names the greatest love: laying down one's life for his friends.

branches.text: Romans 5:8 sets two things side by side: our condition ('sinners') and God's response ('Christ died for us'). The cross is where His love is demonstrated, not merely declared.

title: Who Will Go?
question: What makes Isaiah ready to answer "Here am I; send me"?
blurb: A holy God asks who will go, and one cleansed man dares to volunteer. What got him there?

branches.text: Just before this, Isaiah cried 'Woe is me, for I am ruined' when he saw the King, the LORD of Hosts (Isaiah 6:5). His readiness follows being undone, not feeling worthy.

branches.note: A glowing coal touches his mouth: 'your iniquity is removed and your sin is atoned for.' He is cleansed first, then commissioned.
God to Moses: 'I am sending you.' The same God who asks 'Whom shall I send?' is the one who does the sending.
Jesus still sends: 'Go and make disciples of all nations.' The call to be sent reaches beyond Isaiah.

branches.text: God asks 'Who will go for Us?' and Isaiah freely offers himself: 'Here am I. Send me!' His answer is willing surrender, not coercion.

title: No More Tears?
question: What does God promise to remove forever, and what makes that promise certain?
blurb: A glimpse of the end God is writing: every tear wiped, death undone, and all things made new.

branches.note: The ancient promise this verse echoes: God swallows up death forever and wipes the tears from all faces.
The same promise earlier in Revelation: the Lamb leads them, and God wipes away every tear from their eyes.
Why death can end: "Death has been swallowed up in victory."

branches.text: The list is total: no death, no mourning, no crying, no pain. The reason given is that "the former things have passed away" - the old order itself is gone.

branches.note: The very next verse names the cause: the One on the throne says, "Behold, I make all things new."

title: Who Will See God?
question: What is a "pure" heart, and how does that purity lead to seeing God?
blurb: A clean heart is promised the greatest sight of all - God Himself. What does that purity look like, and how is it received?

branches.note: Who may stand in God's holy place? The one with 'clean hands and a pure heart' - the same pairing of purity with access to God.
David shows the heart is not pure on its own but must be made so: 'Create in me a clean heart, O God.'
Those who hope to see God 'as He is' purify themselves - linking the promise of seeing God directly to purity.
'Without holiness no one will see the Lord' - echoing that purity is what opens the way to God's presence.

branches.text: Across these verses, the 'pure in heart' are not the flawless but those cleansed by God and set on Him - and the reward is the deepest blessing: seeing God Himself.

title: Where Courage Comes From
question: What reason does God give Joshua to be strong and courageous instead of afraid?
blurb: A command to be brave that rests not on Joshua's strength, but on one promise: God goes with him wherever he goes.

branches.text: The command is anchored in a reason: 'for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.' The 'do not be afraid' is not self-generated nerve; it flows from God's presence.

branches.note: Moses gave Israel the same charge: be strong and courageous, do not be afraid, for the LORD your God goes with you and will never leave you nor forsake you.
God repeats the pattern: 'Do not fear, for I am with you... I will strengthen you; I will surely help you.' Fear answered by His presence and His help.
Even walking through the valley of the shadow of death, the psalmist fears no evil 'for You are with me' - courage drawn from the same nearness God promised Joshua.

branches.text: Joshua 1 ties the courage to a task: God commands Joshua to be strong as he leads Israel and keeps the law. The presence empowers the work, rather than removing it.

title: Be Transformed, Not Conformed
question: How does renewing the mind change us, and what does it let us discern?
blurb: One verse, two paths: drift with the world, or be made new from the inside out.

branches.text: The verse sets two paths against each other: "conformed to this world" versus "transformed." The change is inward - it happens "by the renewing of your mind."

branches.note: Put off the old self and "be renewed in the spirit of your minds" - the same inward renewal, putting on the new self.
"Set your minds on things above, not on earthly things" - where the renewed mind chooses to dwell instead of on the world's.
"If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away" - the transformation itself.

branches.text: The renewed mind has a purpose: "then you will be able to test and approve" God's will - discerning what is good, pleasing, and perfect.

title: Fearfully and Wonderfully Made?
question: What does it tell me about God that He made me so carefully, and how should I respond?
blurb: The same God who knit you together knows you completely - and that truth turns wonder into worship.

branches.note: The verse right before names the Maker: God formed my inmost being and knit me together in my mother's womb.
I am wonderfully made because I am made in God's own image - male and female He created them.
God's careful making is also purposeful: He knew and set apart His servant before he was born.

branches.text: The psalmist's response to being so made is praise, not pride - 'I praise You.' Recognizing God's craftsmanship leads upward to worship of the Maker.

title: A Time for Everything?
question: If God sets a season for every purpose, how should we live within His timing rather than our own?
blurb: Every season under heaven has its hour. Trace how Scripture frames God's timing and how we are to meet it.

branches.note: The same chapter says God 'has made everything beautiful in its time' and set eternity in our hearts, yet we cannot fathom the work He has done.
The verse right after the anchor begins the list of paired seasons: 'a time to be born and a time to die.'
David answers the question of timing with trust: 'My times are in Your hands.'

branches.text: The anchor names not random change but ordered purpose: 'a time for every purpose under heaven.' Each season is appointed and set by God.
Read with verse 11, the anchor invites both rest and humility: every season fits God's design, even when we cannot fathom the whole of what He is doing.

title: Sent to Make Disciples
question: What is the church actually sent to do, and on whose authority?
blurb: Before He ascended, Jesus gave one marching order. See what He sent His followers to do, and why.

branches.text: The command is "make disciples" - the main task. "Go," "baptizing," and "teaching" (v.20) describe how it happens. It's not just gaining converts but forming followers.

branches.note: The verse right before: "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me." The mission rests on Jesus' authority - that's why it begins with "Therefore."
The command continues: teach them to obey all Jesus commanded - and His promise, "surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age."
Jesus sends them again: empowered by the Spirit, they witness "in Jerusalem... and to the ends of the earth" - the same reach as "all nations."
The parallel command: "Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature" - the message disciples are sent to carry.
